records.title: Integrin-guided development of defined supramolecular hydrogels for human kidney tubuloid culture.
records.abstract: Tubuloids are epithelial organoids derived from tissue or urine that model tubular nephron segments of the kidney. Their use in preclinical research is limited by dependence on basement membrane extract (BME), a batch-variable animal-derived matrix that reduces reproducibility. Here, we evaluate defined supramolecular ureido-pyrimidinone (UPy) hydrogels as an alternative matrix for tubuloid culture. Re-analysis of a published tubuloid single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset guides selection of two ligands for UPy functionalization to support cell-matrix interactions: the αVβ3-binding cyclic RGD peptide (cRGDfK) and the laminin-derived IKVAV motif. Tubuloids are cultured in UPy gels functionalized with UPy-IKVAV, UPy-cRGDfK, or both, and compared with BME. UPy hydrogels and BME are comparably soft and predominantly elastic. Across experiments, tubuloid lines from six donors are evaluated by confocal imaging, gene expression analysis, and brightfield imaging. UPy-IKVAV hydrogels support cystic tubuloid formation, most closely resemble BME in morphology and lumen formation, and maintain a kidney marker profile comparable to BME after four days, whereas UPy-cRGDfK is associated with more irregular morphologies. Integrin β1 blockade disrupts lumen integrity in BME and UPy-IKVAV hydrogels, supporting a role for β1-mediated cell-matrix interactions in tubuloid organization. UPy-IKVAV hydrogels therefore support viable cystic tubuloids and show promise as a robust matrix for preclinical tubulopathy research.

records.title: From bench to clinic, are organoids ready for modeling drug delivery in brain disease?
records.abstract: Brain diseases remain a significant challenge in the field of modern medicine. The protective function of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) also complicates drug delivery for neurological disorders. However, under certain pathological conditions, the BBB is compromised during the progression of these pathophysiological processes. To integrate with clinical treatments, precise and personalized requirements exist for basic research. Three-dimensional (3D) in vitro systems, particularly organoids, serve as valuable models for preclinical disease research. Starting from the functionality and feasibility of organoids, this review explores their potential roles and applications in brain diseases. It also discusses advanced technologies to overcome in vitro modeling challenges and their applications in evaluating therapeutic strategies and drug delivery. Moreover, with the ability to predict and rapidly screen effective drugs, organoid modeling will be valuable in accelerating the clinical translation of new therapeutics.

records.title: Organoid-Guided Precision Salvage Therapy for Advanced Breast Cancer with Multiple Metastases: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Breast cancer is one of the most prevalent malignancies in women worldwide, and postoperative recurrence, distant metastasis, and multidrug resistance remain major clinical challenges for patients with advanced disease. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs), which have been reported to preserve the histological and molecular characteristics of the original tumor, emerge as a promising platform for accurate drug sensitivity testing. We reported a 77-year-old woman with left-sided breast cancer who developed multiorgan metastases, including lung, brain, liver, and bone, after failing multiple lines of standard therapy. PDOs were successfully established from a liver metastatic biopsy, and subsequent drug sensitivity testing identified gemcitabine and capivasertib as potential sensitive agents. Subsequent PDO-guided salvage therapy achieved partial regression of liver lesions and stable pulmonary disease. Newly detected T2 and T12 vertebral lesions were interpreted as bone pseudoprogression rather than true progressive disease, and bone metastases were assessed as partial response per the MD Anderson criteria. This typical case suggests that PDO-guided drug sensitivity testing may facilitate the identification of potential personalized salvage regimens for patients with refractory metastatic breast cancer. Nevertheless, as derived from a single uncontrolled case, these observations cannot demonstrate the predictive accuracy of PDOs, reversal of treatment resistance or improved clinical outcomes, and require prospective validation.

records.title: Advancing in Sarcoma 3D Modeling: Identification of SRC as an Actionable Vulnerability in Doxorubicin-Resistant Osteosarcoma Organoids.
records.abstract: Tumor organoids have emerged as the most promising avatar to model cancer and to be used as drug testing platform in personalized medicine protocols. The derivation of organoids from epithelial tumors is well established, and their use has proven useful for biomarker discovery, drug screening, and clinical decision support. However, generation of organoids from sarcomas is much less developed and current protocols require further optimization to fully harness their research and clinical potential. In this study, the authors examined the challenges of generating basement membrane extract-based organoids from patient-derived sarcoma samples. Out of 19 samples, 3D structures formed in seven (37%), but none could be propagated beyond the first passage. Alternatively, the authors established expandable organoids from sarcoma xenografts. From 14 xenograft samples, seven (50%) were successfully expanded over multiple passages and biobanked. Notably, xenografts from parental and doxorubicin-resistant 143B osteosarcoma cells yielded long-term cultures suitable for studying drug resistance. Transcriptomic and functional analyses revealed that SRC signaling contributes to doxorubicin resistance in osteosarcoma. Inhibiting SRC with dasatinib restored sensitivity to doxorubicin in vitro and in vivo by downregulating cJUN-mediated ABCB1 expression. These findings support xenograft-derived organoids as a viable platform for modeling sarcoma and investigating therapeutic resistance.

records.title: Engineered organoid platforms for drug delivery evaluation.
records.abstract: Advanced biomaterials and drug delivery systems (DDSs) require human-relevant models that can capture tissue heterogeneity, physiological barriers, and patient-specific therapeutic responses. Conventional two-dimensional cultures and animal models often fail to reproduce these features, contributing to discrepancies between preclinical evaluation and clinical outcomes. Organoids offer three-dimensional, multicellular platforms that partially recapitulate the architecture and functions of human tissues and therefore provide new opportunities for evaluation of material-tissue interactions. This review first outlines the major types of organoids derived from adult stem cells, pluripotent stem cells, and patient tissues. It then discusses engineering strategies, particularly organoid-on-a-chip systems and 3D bioprinting, that introduce controlled fluid flow, mechanical cues, tissue interfaces, and spatial organization to improve physiological relevance, reproducibility, and screening compatibility. Particular emphasis is placed on the emerging use of organoids for assessing DDSs, including tissue penetration, cellular uptake, transport across mucus and blood-brain barrier models, targeting specificity, therapeutic efficacy, and nanomaterial-associated toxicity. Finally, we examine current challenges, including model standardization, vascularization, immune and stromal integration, quantitative validation, scalability, reproducibility, and cost. Integration with defined biomaterials, microfluidics, automated manufacturing, real-time sensing, and computational analysis may establish organoids as complementary and increasingly predictive platforms for biomaterial evaluation, DDS development, safety assessment, and personalized therapy.

records.title: Single-cell perturbation prediction near experimental reproducibility with GENESIS.
records.abstract: Single-cell perturbation atlases now measure cellular responses across millions of cells, but the number of possible combinations of biological contexts, perturbations, doses and other experimental variables make exhaustive measurements infeasible. Here, we present GENESIS (Generative ENErgy-based Single-cell Intervention Simulator), a generative framework that predicts single-cell response distributions directly from the covariates defining an experimental condition. GENESIS uses a lightweight neural network trained with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule for distributions. We introduce an experiment-calibrated evaluation framework in which prediction error is interpreted relative to the reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same condition. Across the Tahoe-100M small-molecule atlas and a large PBMC cytokine atlas, GENESIS significantly outperforms existing generative models and statistical baselines and approaches experimental reproducibility on independently repeated conditions. Importantly, GENESIS remains accurate when trained on only a fraction of the available experimental conditions or cells, and generated profiles recover experimentally observed context-dependent transcriptional programs. At comparable training-cell budgets, GENESIS achieves more accurate predictions when measurements span more experimental conditions rather than profiling fewer conditions more deeply. Together, these findings suggest a complementary strategy for perturbation studies: broader, lower-depth measurements can expand experimental coverage, while GENESIS augments sparsely sampled populations and predicts responses in unmeasured conditions.

records.title: MultiFlow: coupled flow matching for predicting single-cell multiomic perturbation responses in unseen cellular contexts.
records.abstract: Predicting cellular responses to perturbation requires resolving coordinated changes across molecular layers, yet most single-cell perturbation models focus on transcriptional responses alone. Here we present MultiFlow, a coupled flow-matching framework that unifies generation and perturbation prediction of paired gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Through bidirectional information exchange between RNA and ATAC generative flows, MultiFlow learns how their joint distribution depends on cellular context and perturbation identity. Across multiomic generation benchmarks, MultiFlow accurately reproduced paired RNA-ATAC states and their population distributions. In multiome perturbation benchmarks, MultiFlow achieved the strongest overall performance in predicting both gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility perturbation responses, outperforming modality-specific perturbation-prediction methods in cell types whose perturbed states were withheld from training. Joint multiomic modeling further preserved perturbation-induced coordination between modalities, including concordant peak-gene effects and cross-modal cellular neighborhood structure. These results establish MultiFlow as a unified generative framework for modeling paired molecular states and predicting their coordinated perturbation responses across cellular contexts. Code and tutorial of MultiFlow are available at https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.

records.title: Prediction transfer does not imply reliability transfer in single-cell foundation models.
records.abstract: Single-cell foundation models are increasingly transferred across tissues, diseases, perturbation screens, and experimental platforms. Although substantial effort has focused on prediction transfer, it remains unclear whether a model's assessment of its own reliability transfers similarly across biological contexts. Here we define reliability transfer as the ability to transfer an accurate assessment of when model predictions are likely to be correct or incorrect and investigate its behavior across ten perturbation-prediction systems spanning multiple datasets, models, and evaluation settings. We find that reliability transfer varies substantially across source-target pairs and cannot be inferred from predictive performance alone, indicating that prediction transfer and reliability transfer constitute distinct forms of generalization. Analyses of biological annotations, network connectivity, target exposure, and contextual factors reveal that prediction reliability is associated with both shared and context-dependent signals, with their relative importance differing across systems. To characterize this variability, we introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints, context-level signatures derived from strictly cross-fitted SHAP explanations that summarize how reliability estimators combine biological and contextual information when assigning confidence. Across systems, contexts with similar attribution-magnitude fingerprints tended to transfer reliability more successfully, and fingerprint similarity identified transfer sources achieving higher reliability-transfer performance within the observed candidate set. However, these relationships weakened under stricter cross-family transfer settings, indicating that transferable reliability structure remains partly dependent on shared contextual information. Finally, transferred reliability estimators produced different perturbation rankings despite identical perturbation predictions, illustrating a practical consequence of reliability transfer for downstream prioritization. Together, these results establish reliability transfer as a distinct aspect of foundation-model generalization and introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints as a framework for characterizing transferable reliability structure across biological contexts.

records.title: Artificial Cells and Biomimetic Cells: Intelligent Systems Driving a Paradigm Shift in Drug Discovery and Delivery.
records.abstract: The convergence of synthetic biology, materials science, and artificial intelligence drives a transformative shift in biopharmaceutical research, advancing from passive drug carriers to intelligent, programmable therapeutics. This review evaluates artificial and biomimetic cells as a framework that connects fundamental biological discovery with clinical translation. It examines five key technological pathways: membrane-engineered artificial cells, membraneless organelle (MLO) systems, multicompartmental artificial cells, protocell communication networks, and virtual cells. These platforms enable precise regulation of drug stability, targeting, biosynthesis, and adaptive responsiveness. Recent progress includes microenvironment-triggered release, logic-gated intercellular communication, and virtual cell-assisted high-throughput screening and toxicity prediction. Despite these advances, challenges remain in scalable manufacturing, long-term stability, and regulatory adaptation. The integration of closed-loop learning, interpretable models, and advanced biomanufacturing will be essential to position artificial and biomimetic cell systems at the forefront of next-generation precision medicine.

records.title: The Tenocyte from Atom to Cell: A Critical Multiscale Synthesis Linking Collagen Chemistry, Tissue Mechanics, Cell Mechanobiology and Mathematical Modelling.
records.abstract: The tenocyte builds, maintains, senses and degrades one of the most mechanically demanding extracellular matrices in vertebrates, yet the chemical, physical, biological and mathematical descriptions of this system have developed in largely separate literatures. This review examines the tenocyte-matrix unit as a single causal system spanning eight orders of magnitude in length, organised around five transitions: from collagen chemistry to molecular mechanics; from molecule to fibril and fascicle; from tissue loading to the cellular mechanical stimulus; from stimulus to transcription; and from cellular output back to matrix composition. At each transition, we weigh competing hypotheses, identify where evidence is decisive and where it remains correlative, and state the governing equations. We integrate advances from 2021-2026, including single-cell and spatial transcriptomic atlases of human tendons, the establishment of PIEZO1 as a causal regulator of tendon stiffness, and microstructurally derived constitutive models. We argue that tendon homeostasis is a closed-loop control problem, formalised as a mechanostat with an inverted-U dose-response, and that the recurrent pathologies of tendon-tendinopathy, ageing, diabetic stiffening and fibrotic healing are failures of this loop rather than of any single component. An open-source computational companion (tenocyte-virtual-cell) is introduced, and a prioritised research agenda closes the review.

records.title: Primary-Tumor Transcriptomic Signatures Associated with Circulating Tumor Cells Status in Breast Cancer: From CTC-Negative Remodeling to CTC-Associated Metastatic Programs.
records.abstract: Background/Objectives: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) play a central role in metastasis by enabling tumor dissemination through the bloodstream. However, the molecular transition from CTC-negative (CTC-) to CTC-positive (CTC+) states and their associated systemic remodeling remain poorly understood. Methods: We performed a transcriptomic comparison between CTC+, CTC-, and healthy individuals using RNA-seq data and a bioinformatics pipeline. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were subjected to functional enrichment, protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis, survival modeling, and drug perturbation prediction to delineate the molecular determinants of CTC emergence and persistence. Results: Primary tumors from CTC+ patients exhibited distinct transcriptomic profiles characterized by the upregulation of genes involved in PI3K-Akt signaling, extracellular matrix organization, and chromatin regulation (e.g., HDAC1, JUN, KLK10), alongside the downregulation of immune activation pathways, including complement, B-cell receptor (BCR), and T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling. Multi-gene survival models derived from upregulated (KLK10, MEOX2, IRS4, RND2) and downregulated (ALDH3A1, PPP2R2B, IGF1R) hub genes significantly stratified patient outcomes (HR = 1.74-2.44, p < 0.01). In contrast, primary tumors from CTC- patients displayed early systemic transcriptional alterations relative to healthy controls, with 1700+ DEGs linked to MAPK/ERK and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling pathways, suggesting pre-metastatic immune reprogramming even before CTC detection. Drug repurposing analysis identified Trichostatin A, BX-795, and Alvocidib as candidate compounds capable of reversing the CTC+ transcriptional signature. Conclusions: Rather than supporting a strictly binary view of CTC status, our findings are consistent with a transcriptional continuum of distinct yet partially overlapping primary-tumor transcriptional states associated with CTC- and CTC+ status, highlighting a molecular shift from immune suppression to epigenetic adaptation that facilitates hematogenous dissemination. The identified multi-gene prognostic panels and small-molecule candidates provide a foundation for CTC-targeted therapeutic strategies and early detection biomarkers in breast cancer.

records.title: Pharmacophore-Conditioned Diffusion Model for Ligand-Based De Novo Drug Design.
records.abstract: Developing bioactive molecules remains a central, time- and cost-heavy challenge in drug discovery, particularly for novel targets lacking structural or functional data. Pharmacophore modeling presents an alternative for capturing the key features required for molecular bioactivity against a biological target. In this work, we present PharmaDiff, a pharmacophore-conditioned diffusion model for 3D molecular generation. PharmaDiff employs a transformer-based architecture to integrate an atom-based representation of the 3D pharmacophore into the generative process, enabling the precise generation of 3D molecular graphs that align with predefined pharmacophore hypotheses. Through comprehensive testing, PharmaDiff demonstrates superior performance in matching 3D pharmacophore constraints compared to ligand-based drug design methods. Additionally, it achieves higher docking scores across a range of proteins in structure-based drug design, without the need for target protein structures. By integrating pharmacophore modeling with 3D generative techniques, PharmaDiff offers a powerful and flexible framework for rational drug design.

records.title: Programming Targeted Immune Cell Migration Using Orthogonal Chemokine-Receptor Pairs.
records.abstract: Chemokines orchestrate the migration of immune cells throughout the body, but harnessing chemokine signaling to engineer targeted cell trafficking is challenging because of their overlapping interactions and broad expression patterns. Here we used structure-guided protein design to engineer orthogonal chemokine-receptor pairs with minimal crosstalk to native systems. T cells engineered with an ortho-receptor selectively infiltrated tissues producing the ortho-chemokine, in vitro and in vivo. By engineering T cells that both sense and secrete the ortho-chemokine, we generated collective swarming behavior in which pioneer cells attract follower cells via an ortho-chemokine gradient self-organized by positive feedback. By providing orthogonal genetic control over both the generation and sensing of chemokine gradients, this system enables the construction of autonomous spatial targeting programs in engineered cells.

records.title: Reliable and Efficient Agentic Protein Design with Toolset Harnessing.
records.abstract: Computational protein design workflows require the orchestration of multiple tools, data formats, and analysis steps that are often fragmented. Here, we introduce Chaperone, a lightweight and customizable framework that enables seamless integration of RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) [1] with downstream sequence design, structure prediction, and evaluation tools, including ProteinMPNN [2], AlphaFold3 (AF3) [3], and more than 50 other protein design tools. By combining a programmable agent-friendly interface with parallelized execution on high-performance computing systems, Chaperone as a harness enables rapid iteration and scalable exploration of complex protein design workflows. Across an evaluation of nine biomolecular design tasks, we find using Chaperone reduces total token usage relative to baseline agents by 86% and GPU costs by 64%, while increasing the overall computational design pass rate. We demonstrate Chaperone's utility for large-scale design-space exploration through a two-week end-to-end small-molecule binder design campaign, yielding low nanomolar binders to cortisol zero shot. We further demonstrate its versatility across distinct design challenges, including the design of a symmetric 12-subunit self-assembly nanoparticle and a linker that mediates interactions between C2- and D3-symmetric protein complexes to form crystalline assemblies. Together, these results demonstrate how agent harnesses built around standardized tool interfaces can substantially improve the efficiency and success of complex, long-horizon agentic design workflows in biology. We make Chaperone freely available to the community on GitHub: https://github.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone .

records.title: MYC targeted de novo binders impair tumor growth.
records.abstract: MYC is one of the most frequently dysregulated oncogenic drivers across many cancers, yet direct therapeutic targeting has remained difficult because its function is mediated by disordered regions and transient protein-protein interactions. Here we design proteins that bind epitopes within regions of MYC whose sequence is conserved between human and mouse, including intrinsically disordered motifs required for oncogenic activity. In vitro, the designs bind MYC with nanomolar affinity and in cells they engage MYC, disrupt interactions with MAX, and remodel MYC-associated protein complexes. Expression of the binders decreases cell proliferation across diverse MYC-dependent hematopoietic, liver, pancreatic, and patient-derived tumor models, and in an orthotopic pancreatic cancer model, binder-expressing tumor cells were selectively depleted. This work establishes de novo protein design as a generalizable strategy to therapeutically target intrinsically disordered transcription factors. We developed a panel of de novo designed intracellular protein binders that target conserved functional regions of MYC with nanomolar affinity, remodel MYC complexes and interaction networks in cells, suppress proliferation across MYC-dependent cancer models, and are depleted from orthotopic pancreatic tumors in vivo.

records.title: Design and validation of nucleosome binding peptides using BindCraft.
records.abstract: Chromatin is a sophisticated assembly of DNA, RNA and proteins in the nuclei of eukaryotic cells. Protein-protein interactions that govern chromatin function are key regulators of genome activity, making them prime targets for drug discovery. Engineering and modulating these contacts presents a viable pathway for innovative epigenetic therapies. Nucleosomes, the primary structural units of chromatin, feature various interaction interfaces, most notably the acidic patch. This region serves as a critical binding site for numerous chromatin-associated proteins, often via their intrinsically disordered regions. Advances in AI-driven protein design have recently opened new avenues for the rational development of molecules aimed at modulating these chromatin interactions. In this research, we implemented an integrated computational and experimental framework to design and validate peptides targeting the nucleosome acidic patch. We relied on the AI protein design approach implemented in BindCraft to design nucleosome binding peptides. To achieve precise quantitative analysis of these interactions, we refined a donor FRET quenching assay specifically for this application, enabling sensitive and consistent measurement of binding affinities for the designed sequences. We successfully identified peptides with high affinity for the acidic patch on canonical nucleosome core particles. These findings highlight the potential of AI-assisted design for chromatin-targeting agents and establish an effective workflow for their validation, laying the groundwork for synthetic epigenetic modulators and the broader use of protein design in managing 3D genome organization.

records.title: HydroGuard: a controlled release hydrogel-phage delivery system to combat catheter-associated urinary tract infections.
records.abstract: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) rank as the fourth-most significant nosocomial infection globally. CAUTIs account for approximately 80% of hospital-acquired urinary tract infections and represent nearly one-third of all device-associated infections. Urinary catheters serve as a hub for bacteria to form highly resistant biofilms containing pathogens, like Enterococcus (E.) faecalis that reduce effectiveness of the immune system and antibiotic treatments. Therefore, tackling biofilm formation at the catheter surface becomes a crucial step in mitigating CAUTIs. We aim to address E. faecalis biofilm formation by engineering HydroGuard: a Gelatin Methacryloyl (Gel-MA)-based hydrogel injected with bacteriophages, to provide targeted, enzyme-triggered antimicrobial activity. Enterococcus faecalis expresses gelatinase (GelE), a zinc metalloprotease that enhances biofilm formation. GelMA is susceptible to GelE-mediated degradation, enabling enzyme-triggered release of bacteriophages that specifically lyse E. faecalis. For a Biosafety Level 1 proof-of-concept experiment with a well-studied host and phage system, we heterologously expressed GelE in Escherichia (E.) coli DH5α to emulate native E. faecalis expression. This system was tested on dynamically grown biofilms, to simulate similar conditions to the urinary tract. Currently, the E. coli system has shown preliminary inhibition when tested against the hydrogel product, however testing of different phage combinations is needed. Mathematical modelling identified hydrogel crosslinking density as a critical tuneable parameter governing therapeutic availability and predicted nonlinear, degradation-dependent phage release profiles. Sensitivity analyses revealed design trade-offs between structural stability and antimicrobial responsiveness. Together, the biofilm, hydrogel, phage-bacteria, and protein design models form a multiscale computational framework that links biofilm development and environmental conditions to enzyme-mediated hydrogel degradation, phage release, and bacterial suppression. Agent-based biofilm simulations captured emergent spatial dynamics under nutrient, flow, and pH constraints, while a coupled predator-prey model investigated phage-bacteria population dynamics within the degrading GelMA matrix. Computational protein design further explored collagen-like peptide motifs with enhanced folding stability and preserved gelatinase cleavage sites, providing a molecular-level approach to tuneable degradation kinetics. This multiscale framework provides predictive insight into how biofilm conditions, hydrogel degradation, and phage availability interact within the proposed system, while the preliminary experimental observations provide supporting evidence for its feasibility. By integrating synthetic biology, tissue engineering, and modelling, HydroGuard offers a novel, non-antibiotic strategy for CAUTI prevention.

records.title: IP47-13 UCIPredict: Liquid Biopsy-Based Prediction of Immunotherapy Response in Urothelial Carcinoma-Interim Multicenter Results: Erratum.
From Single Cells to the Circulating Tumor Microenvironment: Label-Free Size-Selection and a Morphological Taxonomy for Liquid Biopsy in Cytopathology.
records.abstract: Liquid biopsy-here, the analysis of blood-has often focused on counting solitary circulating tumor cells (CTCs), a readout that omits the multicellular architecture governing metastasis. We summarize a hierarchical morphological taxonomy built on the circulating tumor microenvironment (cTME), then ask what an isolation method must deliver before that taxonomy can be applied at the microscope. We appraised the literature on label-free size-selection (membrane filtration) of whole blood, comparing suction-driven, microfluidic, and gravity-driven platforms for recovery of intact multicellular units and for readability of the resulting preparations by routine cytologic stains and multiplex immunocytochemistry. The critique is paired with the authors' own single-center experience, reported in labeled subsections. Circulating tumor-associated cells (C-TACs) form the functional cellular tier of the cTME: a "mobile niche" comprising a malignant core-solitary CTCs and circulating tumor emboli (CTE)-together with non-malignant supporting partners. Antigen-dependent capture disrupts these units and misses non-epithelial partners, whereas size-selection retains them by size and deformability, independently of surface phenotype. We propose the driving force, and hence the shear imposed on captured cells, as the primary axis for classifying these platforms-a testable hypothesis rather than an established result. Chemo-response profiling of the intact collective by an independent group showed 97% concordance with radiological response in therapy-naïve patients; in our own series, perioperative CTE detection stratified adjuvant chemotherapy benefit in non-small cell lung cancer. Size-selection converts a liquid biopsy into a cytology slide, placing interpretation of the circulating tumor ecosystem within the existing competence of the diagnostic laboratory.

records.title: Liquid biopsy for brain tumors.
records.abstract: Diagnosis and molecular classification of central nervous system (CNS) tumors depend largely on neurosurgical sampling, which may be difficult to obtain and is rarely repeated throughout the disease course. This review examines how liquid biopsy may extend molecular assessment of primary and metastatic CNS tumors beyond the initial tissue specimen. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cell-free DNA can identify diagnostically informative alterations in gliomas, CNS lymphoma, and CNS metastases. Serial sampling can reveal evolving tumor clones and resistance-associated alterations absent from archival tissue. Recent advances in error-corrected sequencing, fragment analysis, and methylation classification broaden the molecular information available from blood and CSF. However, diagnostic yield varies with tumor type, anatomical location, sampling compartment, and assay design, and blood-based detection remains challenging in primary brain tumors. Liquid biopsy may complement tissue diagnosis, imaging, and conventional CSF studies, particularly when repeat tissue sampling is impractical. Prospective validation is needed to establish standardized workflows, clarify the interpretation of negative results, and determine whether molecular findings improve treatment selection and patient outcomes.

records.title: Circular RNAs as promising biomarkers for human diseases: An update for 2018-2025.
records.abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are a class of endogenous non-coding RNAs characterized by their unique covalently closed-loop structure. These molecules are key regulators of gene expression and are closely linked to various human diseases. Due to their intrinsic stability, evolutionary conservation, and tissue-specific expression, circRNAs have emerged as highly promising biomarkers for a wide range of diseases. This review comprehensively synthesizes progress in research from 2018 to 2025 on the biogenesis, nuclear export, and functional mechanisms of circRNAs in human diseases. Further, we update novel detection technologies and methods of circRNAs and discuss the prospects and challenges of translating circRNAs into clinical biomarkers, aiming to facilitate clinical applications.

records.title: Validation of a ctDNA-Based comprehensive genomic profiling panel (IST80 Plus) for advanced non-small cell lung cancer.
records.abstract: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) profiling can complement tissue testing in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), particularly when tissue is unavailable or unable to capture tumor heterogeneity. We evaluated the analytical and clinical performance of Illumina Solid Tumor Panel 80 (IST80 Plus), a focused hybrid-capture next-generation sequencing assay for plasma genomic profiling. Validation included Seraseq-ctDNA reference materials at 2.5% and 0.5% allele frequencies, six external quality-assessment samples, supernatants from three fusion-positive cell lines, and eighteen plasma samples from patients with previously characterized NSCLC alterations. Sensitivity was assessed for small variants, gene fusions, and copy-number variants (CNVs). Quantitative agreement with reference measurements was evaluated using Pearson and Spearman correlations and Bland-Altman analysis. Robustness was explored by downsampling sequencing reads. Among 158 expected variants, 135 were within the panel's reportable range. Overall sensitivity was 95.56% (129/135), comprising 99.06% for small variants (105/106), 88.88% for fusions (16/18), and 72.73% for CNVs (8/11). For 85 detected small variants with available reference allele frequencies, Pearson's r was 0.99 and Spearman's rho was 0.82. Bland-Altman analysis showed minimal bias (0.04%), with 95% limits of agreement from -0.97% to 1.05%. Sensitivity was 98.41% for variants below 1% allele frequency and 100% for variants at or above 1%. All cell-line fusions were detected, as were three of four expected fusions in clinical samples. Following downsampling 50%, 70%, and 90% of the original reads, 81.18%, 85.88%, and 90.59% of 85 reference small variants remained detectable, respectively. Performance was strongest for small variants, whereas lower sensitivity for CNVs was noted. IST80 Plus showed high sensitivity and quantitative accuracy for small variants and reliable fusion detection in ctDNA. Its focused design may support molecular profiling of advanced NSCLC when sample availability and sequencing efficiency are limiting.

records.title: Decoding prognosis: multigene expression assays in breast cancer.
records.abstract: Breast cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related death in women worldwide. In early-stage, hormone receptor-positive/-negative disease, tissue-based multigene expression assays refine prognosis and guide systemic therapy. Axillary nodal status is still determined by clinical examination, imaging and sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB). This narrative review separates prognostic, predictive and nodal-staging information. For MammaPrint, Oncotype DX, PAM50/Prosigna, EndoPredict and Breast Cancer Index, it summarizes the platform, validated population, level of evidence and guideline status. These assays estimate distant-recurrence risk and/or benefit from chemotherapy or extended endocrine therapy; none was developed or validated to predict nodal involvement. The dedicated gene-expression panels for nodal metastasis derive from retrospective or single-cohort studies, lack prospective validation and are not recommended for axillary staging. Liquid biopsy (ctDNA), multi-omics approaches, and cost, access and standardization are also reviewed. The established assays answer narrow, population-specific answers on recurrence and systemic-treatment benefit, not axillary staging; omission of SLNB currently rests on clinical and radiological criteria (SOUND, INSEMA). Nodal signatures remain investigational, and ctDNA and multi-omics approaches are promising but not yet practice-changing, requiring prospective trials showing improved outcomes. Age- and menopausal-status-related chemotherapy effects derive largely from exploratory or subgroup analyses and are hypothesis-generating.
affiliations: School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Lovely Professional University, Phagwara, India.
